title: Not by reputation
hookLine: you can't be a philosopher by reputation; just live by nature (Meditations 8.1)

lines: FAR FROM IT, AND HE SAYS SO.
cards: An emperor sits alone with a notebook he writes to himself. Nobody is watching. He could put down anything he likes about who he is.
Instead he writes a hard sentence: he is far from being a philosopher, and it's plain to others and plain to himself. No excuses, no softening.
That's how book eight of the Meditations begins: not with a triumph, but with an honest confession, and then a way forward.

teach.h: I HAVEN'T LIVED AS A PHILOSOPHER.
teach.b: In Meditations eight, one, Marcus says this thought helps against vanity: you can't claim to have lived your whole life, or even your adult life, as a philosopher.
It's plain to many people, and to yourself, that you're far from it. Your position, he says, works against it. He doesn't soften it.
Then the trap. When you realize you're not what you'd like to be called, there's a temptation to fix the reputation: look more philosophical, talk the part. Marcus closes that door.
Throw away, he says, the question of how you'll seem to others.
Instead, be content to live whatever remains of your life as your nature wants. Where is living well found? In doing what human nature asks.
How? By holding principles from which your actions grow. So he moves the whole question from the label to the practice.
On this path, book eight is about one action at a time, and this is its opening move. You can't become wise by being called wise, or fix a reputation by working on the reputation.
You can only do the next thing well, quietly, again and again.
And Marcus leaves room for it: whatever remains, he says.
Not the whole life. The rest of it. That's enough to work with.

how: Readers of Marcus often take 8.1 as permission to stop worrying about whether they look wise or spiritual, and to put their effort into small actions that follow from their principles.

o: a Stoic who wrote to win fame as a philosopher
a ruler famed in his day as the wisest man alive
the emperor who admitted he was far from a philosopher

games.q: not by reputation — tap the pairs.
p: I haven't lived as a philosopher

s: book eight opens with Marcus admitting he hasn't lived as a philosopher
he says it's plain to others and to himself.
Marcus tells himself to build a better reputation as a philosopher
he says throw away the thought of how you'll seem to others.

games.q: you realize you're not the person you'd like to be known as. what does Marcus do in 8.1?
o: work on how others see him.
drop the label and live as nature asks for the time that remains.
games.why: Meditations 8.1: throw away how you'll seem, and be content to live the rest of your life as your nature wills.

practice: Hold a label you'd like to wear, a good parent, a spiritual person, a hard worker, a kind friend, and notice how much effort goes into seeming that way.
Let it go for the length of this sit, and underneath, find one small action the label points to, something nobody would see. Picture doing it; that's the whole thing.

wordCard.voice: Marcus, who admitted he was far from a philosopher, and turned from the label to living by nature for whatever remained of his life. Today's word.

orig.note: Greek: opinion, reputation, how one seems to others.

carryVoice: Your line: whatever remains of your life. Not the label; the next action. That's five hundred ninety-six.
